definition.text: The food web of life in the sea.

facts.text: Its base is phytoplankton, single-celled algae and plant-like organisms; zooplankton that eat them form the second trophic level.
A typical ocean food chain runs phytoplankton, herbivorous zooplankton, carnivorous zooplankton, filter feeder, predatory vertebrate.
Forage fish sit in the middle of ocean food webs as the main prey of larger fish, seabirds and mammals.
Coastal waters cover about 8 per cent of the ocean but account for about half of all ocean productivity.
Microorganisms play much bigger roles in marine food webs than was once thought.
Ocean acidification damages pteropods and brittle stars at the base of Arctic food webs and threatens those webs from the bottom up.

definition.text: In the sea, the total mass of consumers can exceed that of the producers, turning the usual biomass pyramid upside down.

facts.text: This happens because phytoplankton grow and reproduce fast, so a small mass can sustain a high rate of primary production.
Because of this inversion, zooplankton make up most marine animal biomass.

definition.text: The process by which whales carry nutrients from the ocean depths back up to the surface.

facts.text: Whales feed deep down where krill are found but return regularly to the surface to breathe.

definition.text: An interaction between species in which each gains a net benefit.

facts.text: Examples include plants trading with mycorrhizal fungi, pollination of flowers, seed dispersal by fruit-eating animals, and corals living with zooxanthellae algae.
It contrasts with competition, where both lose fitness, and parasitism, where one benefits at the other's expense.
In mycorrhizae, the plant gives carbohydrates to the fungus in return mainly for phosphate; rhizobia fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates.
Service-resource mutualisms such as pollination, cleaning symbiosis and seed dispersal by animals are common.
Mutualism can evolve from parasitism or commensalism, and can also break down again.
In Three Sisters farming, beans climb cornstalks while fixing nitrogen for the corn.

definition.text: The web of mutualistic links between plants and pollinators, which shows a similar structure across very different ecosystems and continents.

facts.text: Models suggest this structure reduces competition between pollinators and strengthens ecosystem stability.
Pollinators therefore survive harsh conditions together but collapse simultaneously once conditions pass a critical point.

definition.text: Mathematical models that describe how the populations of two mutualist species grow given the benefit each gets from the other.

facts.text: A simple form adapts the Lotka–Volterra equations, adding a positive term for the benefit of the partner species.
In 1989 David Hamilton Wright added saturation: benefits level off at high densities because of handling time.
Without saturation, modelled densities could grow without limit, which carrying capacity makes impossible.
